rationale: A wins because it keeps the live risks inside the story instead of sanding them off: “Patients priced out of branded weight-loss drugs now have a cheaper option — with an FDA warning attached” is a real consumer angle with the landmine visible. B has useful bones, but it turns gaps into claims, especially “Hims & Hers pairs at-home blood testing with prescribing, betting personalization sells better than price,” which invents a strategy the update does not give you. A also makes the unnamed supplier a gating proof point in the strongest angles; B mostly saves that problem for the cleanup section.
gaps_in_A: “branded drugmakers want it stopped” overstates “branded manufacturers have pushed back.” Pushback is grounded; intent to stop it is an inference that needs a document, lawsuit, petition, or quote.
“Hims & Hers is scaling them anyway” is a shade too confident. The facts say launching access, not scale, volume, or rollout size.

The diagnostics angle says telehealth is “running diagnostics.” That is plausible, but it needs the exact operational proof A later asks for: whether blood testing is required and how results change treatment.
gaps_in_B: “patients turn to compounded prescriptions instead” invents patient behavior. The update says patients can get access, not that they are turning to it or switching from branded drugs.
“betting personalization sells better than price” is made up. The facts say blood testing personalizes treatment; they do not say Hims is positioning personalization over price.
“prescription-mill competitors” is an ugly, unsupported flourish. If you want to accuse the category of pill-mill behavior, bring evidence or cut it.
“doubles down” is on the slop blacklist, and here it also overstates the fact pattern. A launch is not automatically a double-down.
